"Getting 195 countries to agree costs billions and takes forever."

No. Getting countries to *implement* things costs billions. Getting them to *sign papers* is surprisingly cheap. Humans love signing papers. It makes them feel important.

## What Treaties Actually Cost

NGO campaign budgets are rarely disclosed publicly, because nonprofits guard their finances the way dragons guard gold. But we know enough to establish something surprising: treaty campaigns run on pocket change.

The **Ottawa Treaty** [@icbl-ottawa-treaty] banning landmines took 14 months. It started with one staff member, Jody Williams, who grew a coalition to over a thousand organizations across 60 countries. Canada committed $100M CAD over 10 years; international donors added $169M in 1997 for mine action. 122 states signed. She won the Nobel Peace Prize.

The **Cluster Munitions Convention** [@cluster-munitions-convention-2008] took about two years. A coalition of NGOs backed by a core group of seven governments got 94 states to sign and over a million stockpiled munitions destroyed.

The **Arms Trade Treaty** [@arms-trade-treaty-2013] took a decade but started with just three supporting governments. The Control Arms coalition [@control-arms-coalition], led by Oxfam and Amnesty International, published 50+ reports and built support until 130 countries signed.

The **Nuclear Ban Treaty** [@ican-nuclear-ban-treaty] also took a decade of campaigning. ICAN ran the entire operation with five staff in a Geneva office, coordinating 468 partner organizations. 122 states voted yes. Another Nobel Peace Prize.

**Pattern**: One woman with a phone convinced 122 countries to ban landmines. Five people in a Geneva office won a Nobel Prize. The NGO costs are a few million dollars per year. Government conference costs add $10-30M. Total to get a treaty signed: **$15-50M**. Your species spends more than that on Super Bowl ads for beer.

### Inflation-Adjusted to 2024 Dollars

Using BLS CPI data [@bls-cpi-inflation-calculator]:

| Treaty (Year) | Original Cost Estimate | 2024 Dollars | Inflation Multiplier |
|:--------------|:----------------------|:-------------|:---------------------|
| Ottawa (1997) | $15-25M | **$30-50M** | ~2.0x |
| Cluster Munitions (2008) | $15-25M | **$23-38M** | ~1.5x |
| Arms Trade Treaty (2013) | $20-30M | **$27-41M** | ~1.35x |
| Nuclear Ban (2017) | $10-20M | **$13-25M** | ~1.25x |

**In today's money**: Treaty campaigns cost roughly **$25-50M** (2024 USD). That's **less than 0.2%** of the implementation cost. Banning landmines: ~$40M to get the signatures, $5B+ to actually dig them up [@icbl-ottawa-treaty]. The paperwork is the cheap part. The not-exploding-anymore part is where it gets expensive.

## Cost for a 1% Health Treaty

This one touches military budgets, the sacred cow of national sovereignty. Suggest moving 1% of the explosion money and politicians look at you like you've asked to borrow their favorite child. So budget 3-4x what landmines cost.

| Phase | Duration | Estimated Cost | Who Pays |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Pre-negotiations**<br>(Coalition building, expert drafts) | 18–24 months | **$8–12M** | Philanthropy (Gates, Open Philanthropy, etc.) + Champion Governments |
| **2. Global Campaign**<br>(Platform, 3.5% consent, media) | 3–5 years | **$45–80M** | Philanthropy + Crowd-funding |
| **3. Diplomatic Process**<br>(Conferences, delegate travel) | 18–30 months | **$15–25M** | Host Governments + UN Trust Fund |
| **4. Ratification Drive**<br>(Legal reviews, parliamentary aid) | 2–4 years | **$5–8M** | Philanthropy |
| **5. Contingency**<br>(Opposition management) | Ongoing | **$10–15M** | Strategic Comms / Lobbying |

**Total: $83–140 Million**

![How long each step takes and how much it costs to convince countries to spend 1 percent of their war budgets on not dying.](/assets/images/treaty-feasibility/treaty-feasibility-section-campaign-roadmap-timeline-bw-academic.jpg)

### The Math

Signing the treaty: ~$83M.
What the treaty unlocks: {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}}/year.
Forever.

That's over 300:1 return on paperwork.

## How to Make Governments Sign Things

Politicians move when they see (a) voters demanding it and (b) political cover. Give them both:

1. **Prove public demand**: Get 3.5% of the population [@3-5-rule] (280M people) to say "yes" with verified identity. Harvard researcher Erica Chenoweth found that every nonviolent campaign [@3-5-rule] with 3.5%+ participation succeeded. That's not activism. That's a mandate. 280 million verified humans is the kind of number that makes politicians suddenly remember they work for you.
2. **Prove it's safe**: Peer-reviewed modeling showing every nation gains more in health savings than it loses in military spending. Politicians need cover the way vampires need darkness. Give them studies to wave around.

![Get 3.5 percent of people to care, show politicians the math won't break anything, and suddenly they have to listen. Democracy has an override button.](/assets/images/treaty-feasibility/treaty-feasibility-section-how-to-make-governments-sign-things-bw-academic.jpg)

### Timeline to "Governments Can't Ignore This"

With ~$60M in seed funding, you can reach "Treaty-Ready" status in **2-3 years**:

- **Platform:** 280M verified supporters (3.5% threshold)
- **Modeling:** Country-by-country impact analysis
- **Coalition:** 120+ supportive NGOs and 5-10 champion governments

Once these assets exist, formal negotiations become inevitable. Not because politicians want them. Because ignoring 280 million people is the kind of career decision that leads to "spending more time with family."

![Two to three years to build the website, run the numbers, and assemble the coalition before you can ask countries to sign. Diplomacy is slow.](/assets/images/treaty-feasibility/treaty-feasibility-section-timeline-to-governments-can-t-ignore-this-bw-academic.jpg)

You aren't buying a treaty.
You're buying the machinery that makes the treaty inevitable.

## Political Success Probability: Economic Analysis {#sec-political-success-probability}

To calculate expected value, you need to estimate the probability this actually works. This section documents the rationale for the **{{< var political_success_probability >}} central estimate** with a **0.1%-10% confidence interval** (and a 25% optimistic scenario ceiling). Yes, the model assumes a 99% chance of failure. It's still a good bet. Stay with me.

![Even if this only has a 1 percent chance of working, it saves 503 times more lives per dollar than bed nets. Math is strange.](/assets/images/treaty-feasibility/treaty-feasibility-section-political-success-probability-economi-bw-academic.jpg)

Even at {{< var political_success_probability >}} probability of success, this intervention's expected cost per DALY ({{< var treaty_expected_cost_per_daly >}}) is still **{{< var treaty_expected_vs_bed_nets_multiplier >}} more cost-effective** than malaria bed nets ({{< var bed_nets_cost_per_daly >}}/DALY). Bed nets are the gold standard of global health interventions.

### Historical Precedents (The Depressing Table)

| Commitment | Target | Actually Did It? | Duration | Notes |
|:-----------|:-------|:------------------|:---------|:------|
| **0.7% ODA Target** | 0.7% of GNI to foreign aid | ~20% of countries | 50+ years | Scandinavia and Germany. That's basically it. |
| **Kyoto Protocol** | Binding emissions targets | ~55% initially, then collapse | 1997-2012 | US never ratified. Canada withdrew. Classic. |
| **Paris Agreement** | Non-binding pledges | ~15-25% on track | 2015-present | 195 countries signed. Maybe 40 meant it. |
| **NATO 2% GDP Defense** | 2% of GDP on defense | ~32% of members | Since 2014 | Even "we might get invaded" wasn't enough |
| **EU Stability Pact** | 3% deficit, 60% debt | Routinely violated | Since 1997 | France and Germany broke their own rule |

**Pattern**: International financial commitments achieve **<25% meaningful compliance**. Your species signs things and then doesn't do them. It's like a New Year's resolution, but for geopolitics.

### Why a 1% Treaty is Harder Than Most Precedents

Let's be honest about the obstacles. This is not a chapter written by someone trying to sell you something. (It is. But at least it's honest about the hard parts.)

1. **Touches military budgets**: Politicians would rather discuss their browser history than their defense budget.
2. **Requires ongoing annual allocation**: Not a one-time signature like banning a weapon. It's a gym membership for peace. Monthly. Forever.
3. **No immediate security threat**: Unlike NATO spending increases post-Ukraine. Hard to motivate governments without an active catastrophe, even though {{< var global_disease_deaths_daily >}} apparently doesn't qualify as one.
4. **Novel mechanism**: Military-to-health reallocation has never been done. Humans are suspicious of things they haven't tried before, which is odd for a species that also invented bungee jumping.
5. **Coordination problem**: Benefits require critical mass. Nobody wants to go first. Everybody wants to go second.

### Why a 1% Treaty Might Beat the Odds

![Five reasons countries might sign: saves money, voters want it, legal precedent exists, morally defensible, and everyone else is doing it.](/assets/images/treaty-feasibility/treaty-feasibility-section-why-a-1-treaty-might-beat-the-odds-bw-academic.jpg)

1. **Self-funding**: Creates health dividends that exceed the "cost." You make money doing this. That's unusual for moral obligations.
2. **Bipartisan appeal**: "Should we cure more diseases?" polls well across every political spectrum. Shocking, I know.
3. **Referendum pathway**: Can bypass government resistance through direct democracy. Politicians hate this one weird trick.
4. **Visible beneficiaries**: {{< var global_disease_deaths_daily >}}. Hard to argue with the body count.
5. **Network effects**: Each signing country makes the next more likely. Peer pressure: humanity's most reliable technology.

### Probability Estimates

Economists would find the following defensible (and economists find very little defensible):

| Scenario | Probability | Translation |
|:---------|:------------|:----------|
| **Pessimistic floor** | 0.1% | Everything goes wrong. Global crises. Political gridlock. Asteroid, possibly. |
| **Conservative central** | {{< var political_success_probability >}} | 99% chance of failure. Still {{< var treaty_expected_vs_bed_nets_multiplier >}} better than bed nets. |
| **Optimistic ceiling** | 25% | A major crisis opens a political window. Or humans just... decide to be smart for once. |

**The model uses**: Central estimate **{{< var political_success_probability >}}**, 95% CI **[0.1%, 10%]**

### Expected Value (Even When You Assume Failure)

![Worst case: you wasted less money than bed nets cost. Best case: you ended most diseases. Risk-reward has never been clearer.](/assets/images/treaty-feasibility/treaty-feasibility-section-expected-value-implications-bw-academic.jpg)

At {{< var political_success_probability >}} probability of success:

- **Expected ROI**: {{< var treaty_expected_roi_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}}:1 (still positive, even assuming near-certain failure)
- **Expected cost per DALY**: {{< var treaty_expected_cost_per_daly >}} ({{< var treaty_expected_vs_bed_nets_multiplier >}} better than bed nets at {{< var bed_nets_cost_per_daly >}}/DALY)

Downside: capped at ~{{< var treaty_campaign_total_cost >}}. You lose the cost of a nice yacht.
Upside: unbounded. You cure most diseases.

Even assuming a 99% chance of total failure, this beats the gold standard of global health interventions. The math doesn't care about your pessimism.

## Why The Treaty Won't Stop at 1%

Most international commitments stagnate after signing. You saw the depressing table. 0.7% ODA targets unmet for 50+ years. Kyoto abandoned. Paris missed. Your track record with follow-through makes goldfish look disciplined. So why would a 1% health treaty be any different?

**Because this time, people get paid.**

The [80/10/10 funding structure](../appendix/incentive-alignment-bonds-paper.qmd) allocates {{< var iab_political_incentive_funding_pct >}} of treaty funding ({{< var iab_political_incentive_funding_annual >}}/year at 1%) to [Incentive Alignment Bonds](../appendix/incentive-alignment-bonds-paper.qmd). These are securities that pay out when treaties *expand*, not just maintain. In other words: people get rich when more diseases get cured. Finally, a financial instrument that isn't morally bankrupt.

### The Expansion Mechanism

| Treaty Level | Annual IAB Pool | Political Pressure | Historical Comparison |
|:-------------|:----------------|:-------------------|:---------------------|
| 1% | $2.72B/year | Strong | 10x largest NGO budgets |
| 2% | $5.44B/year | Very strong | Nation-state level |
| 5% | $13.6B/year | Overwhelming | Major industry lobby |
| 10% | $27.2B/year | Unstoppable | No precedent |

### Why This Differs from Every Other Treaty

**0.7% ODA failed** because nobody made money when countries complied. The NGOs pushing for compliance have small budgets, compete with each other, and run on guilt. Guilt has terrible fuel efficiency.

![Old way: charities beg governments. New way: investors get paid when governments cooperate. Greed works faster than guilt.](/assets/images/treaty-feasibility/treaty-feasibility-section-why-this-differs-from-stagnant-treaties-bw-academic.jpg)

**The 1% health treaty creates its own expansion lobby.** Bond holders profit when the treaty expands to 2%, then 5%, then 10%. These aren't activists you can ignore at a dinner party. They're investors with quarterly earnings calls about curing diseases.

### The Ratchet Effect

Once 1% passes:
1. **$2.72B/year** flows to IAB holders pushing for 2%
2. When 2% passes, **$5.44B/year** pushes for 5%
3. When 5% passes, **$13.6B/year** pushes for 10%
4. The political pressure for expansion *accelerates* with each success

Most treaties are gym memberships purchased in January and abandoned by February. IABs are the opposite: the constituency for expansion *grows* with each success. Greed doesn't take holidays.

### Long-Term Feasibility

![Path one: treaty fizzles. Path two: financial incentives make it grow to $2.7 trillion like compound interest for not dying.](/assets/images/treaty-feasibility/treaty-feasibility-section-long-term-feasibility-bw-academic.jpg)

With IABs, the {{< var iab_political_incentive_funding_pct >}} allocation creates a perpetual political engine. A machine that runs on greed and outputs health. Embarrassing, but effective.

Without IABs, this joins Kyoto in the Museum of Things Humanity Promised to Do and Then Didn't.
